title: Mata Khivi's kitchen
hookLine: Guru Angad's wife runs the langar and is remembered for serving rich rice pudding to all

cards: Some of a family's deepest teaching happens in the kitchen, nowhere near a classroom or a place of worship. Who gets fed first. Whether there's always room for one more.
What you do when someone shows up hungry and unannounced. At Khadur, while Guru Angad taught the letters, another teacher was at work, and her classroom was a kitchen. Her name was Mata Khivi.

Mata means mother, a title of respect. She was Guru Angad's wife, and she ran the langar, the free community kitchen where everyone who came was fed, sitting side by side. Today, what she served, and what it taught.

teach.h: MATA KHIVI IS IN THE SCRIPTURE.
teach.b: Mata Khivi is in the scripture.
In the Guru Granth Sahib, a ballad by two of the Gurus' musicians, Satta and Balvand, says, in paraphrase, that Khivi is a good woman who gives cool, leafy shade to everyone, like a great tree.

In her kitchen, it says, the Guru's bounty is shared out, and the kheer, rice pudding rich with ghee, the clarified butter, tastes like nectar. A book of hymns about God honors a woman for her cooking and her kindness.
That's not a small thing. It says the kitchen is holy ground too. Why rice pudding?
In that time and place, kheer made with ghee was a rich food, the kind served at celebrations or to honored guests, not handed out to whoever walked in.
Mata Khivi served the good stuff to everyone, the laborer and the landlord at the same meal. Remember Lalo's bread? That was honest food earned by hard work.
This is the other side of the same teaching: when you share, share the best you have.
Sikh tradition remembers Mata Khivi as one of the people who made the langar what it is today, not just a charity meal but a table where everyone is an honored guest.
A gurdwara kitchen stirring a pot of dal for strangers tonight is, in some way, still her kitchen.

how: Sikhs honor Mata Khivi as a shaper of the langar, the free kitchen at the gurdwara, where volunteers cook and serve anyone who comes, seated together; kheer is still often served there.

o: a sweet bread made for festivals
a lentil stew cooked for guests

games.q: what's inside the kitchen — tap the pairs.
p: sang her praise in the scripture

s: no woman of the Gurus' time is named in the Sikh scripture
Mata Khivi is named, in the ballad of Satta and Balvand.
Mata Khivi served plain food to the poor and rich food to guests
she served the rich kheer to everyone alike.
the ballad compares her to the shade of a great tree
cool, leafy shade for everyone who comes.

games.q: you're running a free kitchen. a laborer and a landlord sit down side by side. you have plain bread and a pot of rich rice pudding. what do you serve?
o: pudding to the landlord, bread to the laborer.
bread to both, to keep it fair.
games.why: Mata Khivi is remembered for serving the rich kheer to all. share the best you have, and everyone is an honored guest.

practice: Think of someone you could give a sweet thing: a coworker, a neighbor, the person who delivers your mail, someone at home. Not the leftover cookie; the good one, and picture their face as you hand it over.
If you can't give food, give something else sweet: a real compliment, a thank-you note.

wordCard.voice: Kheer. The rich rice pudding Mata Khivi served to everyone in the langar at Khadur, and for which she is honored by name in the scripture.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kheer, rice pudding cooked in milk; the ballad says hers was rich with ghee.

carryVoice: Your line: the kitchen is a teacher. Tomorrow, the wrestling ground at Khadur. That's forty-six days.
